_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- North Carolina holiday calendars. Loaded through
add_holidays alongside sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_northcarolina.json.
== THIS CALENDAR IS A COURT CLOSURE SCHEDULE, NOT A HOLIDAY STATUTE, AND THAT
READ THIS BEFORE 'FIXING' ANY ENTRY AGAINST G.S. 103-4. N.C. R. Civ. P. 6(a)
-- G.S. 1A-1, Rule 6(a) -- rolls a last day off "a Saturday, Sunday or a legal
holiday WHEN THE COURTHOUSE IS CLOSED FOR TRANSACTIONS". It never cites
G.S. 103-4 and the qualifier is not decoration: it makes actual closure the
test. So the operative source is the Judicial Branch's published closure
schedule, read from nccourts.gov/holiday-schedule on 2026-08-25, and NOT the
statutory list.
THE TWO LISTS ARE VERY DIFFERENT AND THE STATUTE IS THE DANGEROUS ONE.
G.S. 103-4(a) declares as legal public holidays, among others: Robert E. Lee's
Birthday (19 January), Greek Independence Day (25 March), the anniversary of
the Halifax Resolves (12 April), Confederate Memorial Day (10 May), the
anniversary of the Mecklenburg Declaration (20 May), Washington's Birthday
(third Monday in February), First Responders Day (11 September), Columbus Day
(second Monday in October), Yom Kippur, and the Tuesday after the first Monday
in November in general election years. THE JUDICIAL BRANCH CLOSES FOR NONE OF
THEM. Encoding G.S. 103-4 would add roughly nine holidays a year that no
courthouse observes, and every one of them would roll a deadline LATER than the
true date -- the direction that misses a filing.
NOTE THIS INVERTS THE STANDING GUIDANCE IN api/_lib/deadline-engine.js. That
note, written for Pennsylvania, says to encode the statute and disclose the
divergence when a published closure schedule is broader than the statutory
list. Pennsylvania's rule tests whether a day is "made a legal holiday by the
laws of this Commonwealth" -- a statutory test -- so encoding the statute is
right THERE. North Carolina's rule tests closure, so encoding the statute is
wrong HERE. The guidance is conditional on the rule's own test, and the engine
note has been amended to say so.
== COVERAGE IS 2026-2027 ONLY, AND THAT IS A PROPERTY OF THE SOURCE =========
Every other jurisdiction in this engine carries 2026-2031. The NCAOC publishes
dated closure schedules roughly two years forward, and 2028 was not published
as of 2026-08-25. A North Carolina computation that crosses into 2028 REFUSES
with NOT_PROVISIONED rather than being computed against a year that is not
known. THIS CALENDAR NEEDS RE-RUNNING EACH YEAR as NCAOC publishes, which is
not true of any other jurisdiction here.
DO NOT EXTEND IT BY COMPUTATION. The Christmas and Thanksgiving blocks are
administrative allocations, not derivable from any rule: Christmas is THREE
days (2026: 24, 25 and 28 December; 2027: 23, 24 and 27 December) and
Thanksgiving is TWO. Nothing in G.S. 103-4 or in Rule 6 produces those dates.
A generated North Carolina calendar would be wrong, and it would be wrong in
both directions at once.
== ONE KNOWN GAP AT THE 2027 YEAR BOUNDARY, AND IT FAILS EARLY =============
1 January 2028 is a Saturday. On the Judicial Branch's own stated convention --
"When a designated holiday falls on Saturday, the preceding Friday will be
observed" -- New Year's Day 2028 would be observed on Friday 31 December 2027,
a date belonging to this 2027 calendar. It is NOT included, because the 2028
schedule that would establish it has not been published and inventing it would
be encoding a prediction. Consequence: a deadline landing on 31 December 2027
does not roll and is computed EARLIER than it may truly be, which files early.
Add it when NCAOC publishes 2028.
Rule 6(a) says "the courthouse", singular, and North Carolina's trial courts
sit county by county. A county courthouse closed for weather, a local
emergency or a county-specific event is closed for transactions and its
closure is a Rule 6(a) holiday for that court. None of that is enumerable in
advance and none of it is below. This is the same treatment already given to
Michigan, whose MCR 8.110(D)(2)(c) expressly permits local administrative
orders modifying the schedule. A deadline computed across a local closure is
EARLY, never late.
Rule 6(a) also provides that "A half holiday shall be considered as other days
and not as a holiday." No half holiday appears below, by that instruction.

authority.note: Read 2026-08-25 from the North Carolina Judicial Branch's published holiday schedule at nccourts.gov/holiday-schedule. THIS IS A CLOSURE SCHEDULE, NOT G.S. 103-4, because N.C. R. Civ. P. 6(a) rolls off "a legal holiday when the courthouse is closed for transactions" -- closure is the rule's own test and the statute is never cited. G.S. 103-4 lists roughly nine further days (Robert E. Lee's Birthday, Greek Independence Day, Halifax Resolves, Confederate Memorial Day, Mecklenburg Declaration, Washington's Birthday, First Responders Day, Columbus Day, Yom Kippur, general election day) for which the Judicial Branch does NOT close; encoding them would push deadlines LATE. Twelve days a year, with Thanksgiving at two days and Christmas at three, both allocated administratively and NOT derivable from any rule. Weekend convention per the Judicial Branch: Saturday -> preceding Friday, Sunday -> following Monday. County-level closures (weather, local emergency) are Rule 6(a) holidays for that courthouse and are not enumerable; a deadline computed across one is EARLY, never late. The page is JavaScript-rendered and refuses plain automated fetches, so it was read in a real browser.
